The suggestion which I have to make is one the merit of which the Prime Minister has already endorsed some time ago. The question I have in mind is one which we have raised when we have had other bills before us appointing new ministers to the cabinet, namely, the technical question concerning the authority for paying the tax-free $2,000 car allowance to cabinet ministers. As the Prime Minister and the committee are aware, there is no reference to that item in the section now before us. It provides only for the salary of $10,000 a year. Those who have followed this matter realize that an item in the Appropriation Act of 1931, I believe it was, provided in that year for a car allowance to each cabinet minister in the amount of $2,000.
On previous occasions we have discussed the merits of relying on that item. It still perplexes me, but I know that the authorities have ruled it is proper to rely on that item and to continue paying the $2,000 for this purpose each year. My point is that that

was an appropriation act for that particular year which voted a precise sum of money which was spent that year but has since been spent over and over again, ft is treated by the financial people, however, as a continuing item. I believe it is fair to say that the Prime Minister agreed with me when I raised the point on an earlier occasion, and said it was one of the things that might well be tidied up. I believe that is the very phrase the Prime Minister used. On subsequent occasions I have asked if this bit of tidying up had been dealt with, and the answer so far has been in the negative.
I would point out that we are about to receive, some time this spring we hope, the new Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952. I have not seen them, but it would be my guess that the Appropriation Act of 1931 is not brought forward in the revised statutes of 1952. In general terms the revised statutes of 1952 will be the law of the country from that time forward. In this instance the government will be going back beyond these revised statutes to that old Appropriation Act of 1931 for the purpose of paying this item. It does seem to me that it should be put on a better basis.
I am not arguing now about the question of the amount being paid. I am arguing about the way in which it is being handled. We all felt that it was desirable to have that recognition retained in the title as a proclamation of the historical, traditional link between this country and the United Kingdom; and the same feelings were entertained by the other two prime ministers with respect to their countries.
The question then arose whether it would be proper to have in the title we would use the traditional words, "by the grace of God", sovereign. Mr. Chairman, it was a nost moving address to which we have just .istened. It is evidence of the strength of ;he parliamentary system that while we may De separated in smaller things, in respect to jur system of government and to the unity hat is provided by the crown there is no livision, there is no diversity of opinion, here is but a common devotion. It is on pccasions like this that parliament rises to ts greatest heights. As we listened to the Prime Minister without regard to party considerations this parliament became cathedral ,n devotion to our history, to our heritage and to our common pursuit of freedom.
As I listened to the Prime Minister referring ;o the diversity of the membership within the commonwealth, and in particular to the rather anomalous position of India, I could not help Dut remember that events of the last few i^ears have established clearly that while [ndia, becoming a member in the circumstances under which she did, seemed in essence to destroy the power of this com-nonwealth, it has really meant its strengthening and has given to the commonwealth a representation in Asia that may well stand as a rampart against the advance of communism which would destroy the system in which we believe.
The change in the Queen's title is an event af great importance. Parliament assumes the responsibility of approving or disapproving the title suggested by the prime ministers' meeting in London. The reason for this lates back to the imperial conference of 1930 when the various members of the British commonwealth decided that the assent of the parliaments of all the dominions, as well as of the parliament of the United Kingdom, was required in order to change the name.
The royal style and title has been changed through the ages as the concept of government has changed. Parliament walks with history in the changes that have taken place. The title of the first sovereign of the United Kingdom was King of the English, which was established by King Egbert in the ninth century. There was a further change a thousand years ago by King Athelstan when he adopted the title King of Britain. Henry VIII added Defender of the Faith. There were no changes then for several centuries until in 1800, when the act of union with
TMr. St. Laurent.]
Ireland made necessary a change in the title of the British sovereign.
It is of interest to recall that for more than three hundred years the sovereign bore the title not only of Defender of the Faith but also of King of France. It was not until 152 years ago that the British sovereigns altered their royal style and title in that regard and removed, from the British coat of arms, the arms of France.
The next change, as I remember my history, was in the 1870's when India became an empire within the British empire. In 1901 the royal title was changed in order to include the British dominions beyond the seas. Then in 1927 a further change took place when Ireland withdrew and an alteration was made in the title to cover that situation.
So the changes have taken place. One of the most moving things about these changes is the fact that the title of every British monarch has never been a boastful one, or one of pomp in words. That is one of the abiding things of the title now established, its freedom from anything in the nature of boastful pride. It is simple, moving and direct.
Freedom owes much to the British monarchy. When one indulges in the "ifs" of history it makes one wonder what might have happened to freedom in the world had Cromwell succeeded in forever abolishing the British monarchy. Had he done so there would never have been the British commonwealth or the commonwealth as it is known now, for it would have been impossible to bind together the various races and religions in all parts of the world but for the centralizing mystic influence of the crown. The commonwealth typifies unity in diversity. Was there ever a more anomalous condition of affairs than this crown with its symbolism, the queen of each of the various parts of the commonwealth, indivisible yet divisible?. Yet that very anomaly permits of constitutional flexibility permitting of a living, vital organism in constitutional and parliamentary development.
The Prime Minister spoke of the meaning of our citizenship. One of the major reasons that I wanted to come to parliament was that I wanted to do my part to assure within this country a Canadian feeling that would deny a hyphenated citizenship while at the same time maintaining pride in the racial origin of one's father and one's mother. The first speech I made in parliament was to that effect, urging equality of Canadians regardless of race, and I expressed the hope that those who served in two world wars would have the right to be in days of peace what

they were in war, namely to be Canadians without any hyphenate consideration whatsoever. Their pride in war was on their. shoulder strap-"Canada".
We are building that type of Canada. Year by year we are building in stronger unity. We in Canada represent something that the world must ultimately attain, a realization that it is not one's surname that makes for citizenship, but service and devotion to the public cause. We are building in unity and we are denying discrimination based on race or creed. What we are doing here has within it the elements of what is necessary to be achieved in the world.
Communism, some say, marches on an empty stomach, but communism also marches because all of us have been guilty too often of the practice of the luxury of mental discrimination against those who belong to other races. As communism marches, one of the greatest bulwarks against it is the fact that we within this commonwealth spread all over the world have practised and are practising in ever widening measure our belief in the sacredness of the human personality and the equality of all without regard to race. Asia is in a desperate situation as she faces the forces of communism; but if the concept of the commonwealth, which has now been proven to be the right one, can be grasped by the minds of the coloured races everywhere, the commonwealth shall indeed have greater days in the future than in all its glorious history.
It is not in the name or title of the sovereign, it is not in title that the strength of our country within the commonwealth consists. It is not in constitutions, not in unification under a central authority that the commonwealth is strong and vital, but it is in that relationship of heart and soul to which the Prime Minister referred as having been characteristic of the last meeting of the prime ministers in London.
I want to see the commonwealth strengthened in heart and soul. In the last few days we have shown what our attitude is not only to the people of Britain but also to the people of Holland and Belgium whence many of our citizens have come. The members of the commonwealth are united in their devotion to freedom. Each realizes that each is indeed each other's keeper, each is filled with pride in our heritage in this year of the coronation and the formal dedication of Her Majesty to the service of her peoples everywhere.
I pass this on to the Prime Minister through you, sir, as an idea that I have embraced, and I ask him whether it would not be in accord-

One of the most interesting points of symbolism in it, as I see it, is the fact that we in parliament have the privilege and are called upon to deal with a measure of this kind. To me the most important and significant aspect of the parliamentary form of government is the fact that we have the executive branch of the government here on the floor of parliament with the rest of us who represent the people of the constituencies of this country. Obviously I have in mind the fact that in some countries there are other forms of government where the executive is apart from the elected representatives of the people. We on the floor of parliament have many a quarrel with the executive, and we shall no doubt continue to have these quarrels. Nevertheless, my point is that it is a matter of great satisfaction to us, and it is a matter of great significance to the people of Canada, that we have the executive here on the floor of parliament, where we can get at the heads of the various departments of government and where they must accept their responsibility to parliament.
So, Mr. Chairman, as I say, this bill is one that has symbolism in that it goes beyond the subject matter that is covered in the actual terms of the clauses now before us. We should on occasions such as this remind ourselves of the privilege that is ours of having inherited the parliamentary system

Our desire today is not to "vanquish enemies"; our desire today is to make friends out of enemies and to build a world of peace and human accord the world around.
I do not propose it as something which needs to be attended to overnight but I would hope that thought might be given to considering the language of that prayer and bringing it more into line with the spirit and aims- in terms of peace and human brotherhood- that characterize the various nations of this commonwealth.

We have had further evidences of that reality in the manner in which the people of Canada now join in welcoming the coronation of this young lady as the living embodiment of those decencies that are represented in the occupation of that throne. The reality is one of respect for the great traditions which were never greater than they are today. The reality is one of loyalty and affection for an institution that has come to mean so much to us and to the whole free world. It is in institutions of this kind that the hope of people now enslaved depends in a great measure at this hour.
We might differ as to the exact wording that would best express our own thoughts as to this remarkable association, but it is recognized by hon. members of this house that the measure now before us interprets that agreement which the Prime Minister has described as resulting from the discussions which took place in London last December. That agreement having been reached and the new titles having been announced, there would seem to be little advantage to be gained in seeking to redefine what is not so much a matter of definition as rather one of affection, respect and loyalty.
For that reason it is not my thought to deal with any of those discussions which

doubtless took place at the time the prime ministers met last December. Undoubtedly the different names and titles that might be in our minds today were before them. Agreement was reached, and to us that agreement is a matter of great importance at this time. I am sure that we all join with the Prime Minister, the hon. member for Lake Centre and the others who have spoken in recalling with real sentiments of satisfaction the fact that the great nation of India, with the second largest population of any nation in the world, has seen fit to continue the association of that great and historic people with the other nations which make up the commonwealth. So also has the nation of Pakistan, with a population more than six times that of Canada, decided to continue that association under these new terms.
Whether we might have felt some measure of satisfaction if other names and titles had been chosen, the reality remains that India and Pakistan as well as all the other nations of the commonwealth have continued as members of this great fellowship of free people; and to every one of us today that is the most important fact before us. If, out of that measure of common agreement which has been reached, the foundation has been laid for a continuing association of a similar type of democracy in Asia, in Europe, in North America and in Australasia, then undoubtedly one of the greatest achievements in all history will have been accomplished. I should think that nothing could offer a better example to the rest of the peoples than to see India, Pakistan and the other nations and territories of Asia joining with us in this ancient fellowship at this time under whatever names and titles may be chosen. For us the reality-the Queen-which is expressed in these terms is the reality we wish to preserve.

It was in 1949 that agreement was reached in London that this phrase, bead of the commonwealth, should describe


a new relationship of the crown to the commonwealth which was made necessary by the inclusion, in the commonwealth, of a republic. I recall, because I had the great privilege of being present at these discussions, the very earnest effort that was made at that time, in the best traditions of adaptability and flexibility in the commonwealth association, to find an expression-something which would certainly not be possible in strict legality as it would have been conceived by constitutional lawyers twenty years ago-under which we could include in our commonwealth association a country with the largest group of people in that association, India, which had declared itself a republic.
That was done, and the expression "head of the commonwealth" was then used in proclaiming the accession of Queen Elizabeth II in the United Kingdom. This is, as I have said, one of the principal common elements in the varying titles which have now been agreed upon. Our Queen then, Mr. Chairman, is head of a commonwealth whose members include a republic of which she is not Queen and in which she has no constitutional function to perform. That, I suggest, is striking evidence not only of the adaptability of the commonwealth to changing conditions but of the political realism and ingenuity of the peoples and the governments who make up the commonwealth. It is striking evidence of the adaptability of this association to new conditions and of our power to adjust our constitutional practices and our constitutional procedures to these new conditions. It is one more proof, if proof is needed, that membership in the commonwealth imposes no limitation whatever on a nation's control over all its affairs, including its constitutional development as a republic or as a monarchy.
For certain members of the commonwealth -and this certainly includes Canada-the monarchical form is preferable because it symbolizes in a very real way the unbroken continuity in our history and the development of our political institutions from Magna Carta to the session of the House of Commons in Ottawa today. The crown under the monarchical principle also lends, I think, stability and dignity to our national life, and I am sure we all agree that that is important in a democratic system based on the free and active play of party controversies. The crown as head of the state and as represented in our country, standing above all such controversies, commanding and deserving the respect and loyalty and affection of us all, ensures a more solid and secure

Yet it is good to know that the commonwealth, with its monarchical and its republican membership, is flexible enough to include Asian as well as western members, and a republic as well as monarchies. This becomes an essential feature in the new and important role which the commonwealth now performs, a bridge between the west and Asia at a time when there are too few such bridges and when they are more important to -the world's history than ever before. All those who believe in co-operation between states must be heartened by this new opportunity of service which is afforded the members of the commonwealth family, and they must be heartened also by the fact the crown will continue to play a vital part in that association in the future as it has in the past.
At London, as I have said, it was agreed last December to differ, if necessary, in the titles and style of the crown, but we all agreed, without difficulty and without difference, in respect of our determination to pursue within the commonwealth those ideals for which the crown so finely stands-peace, dignity and ordered progress.

South Saskatchewan River Project

Mr. Speaker, this motion affords to members of parliament an opportunity to assert their traditional right to bring before the executive any matter that they believe is of interest to the people of their country, the basis being that supply shall not be granted until causes of complaint have been fully discussed. It is in that spirit I intend to deal with a matter of transcendent importance to the people of western Canada, and in particular the peoples of the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.
I bring this matter up on this occasion to give parliament an opportunity of discussing a question pertinent to the prosperity of western Canada. I commence by pointing out that the questions of irrigation and of power in Saskatchewan and in western Canada generally have been matters of constant reference for several generations. I go back to the days of the Palliser expedition and also to the recommendations made as far back as 1856, when even then it was suggested, in the diaries of early explorers, that the area which we now know as the Palliser triangle, extending as well beyond Canada in the general direction of Salt Lake City, might in the future be subject to settlement; but that in order to settle it there would be required the benefits of irrigation for the reason that from generation to generation, periodically, drought has come to that area.
This matter has been before the House of Commons on a number of occasions. It has been discussed throughout the years in the legislature of the province of Saskatchewan. As I say, it has been brought to the House of Commons periodically since 1938 when the late John R. MacNicol dealt at length with the problems of irrigation. It has been before us year by year since that time.
I am not going to go into the references by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) throughout the years, although that could be done later on if necessary. Throughout the years he has been constantly bringing to the attention of the people of Saskatchewan the need for irrigation, the demand for power, and has pictured Saskatchewan and other areas within the Palliser triangle as areas that might well in future be of the type of the Essen area in Germany, power resulting in industrial development and irrigation resulting in areas arid today blooming as the rose,
As far back as 1946 the minister, speaking at a meeting that year, as reported in the Regina Leader-Post of April 27, said:
The dominion government had already mapped out a program, and it was a program involving

South Saskatchewan River Project $110 million. This would be used largely in providing for the storage of water and partly for the distribution of this water where needed.
The dominion government thus did not need the endorsation of the South Saskatchewan river development association to begin work on the South Saskatchewan river. It had already decided to go through with it.
Later in the summer of 1946, again speaking in the province of Saskatchewan, the Minister of Agriculture was reported as saying:
-a decision would be reached on where the dam on the South Saskatchewan should be placed. It would be on one of three sites between the Elbow and Saskatchewan.
As soon as the site had been finally decided upon, contracts would be let and work would proceed immediately.
Throughout the years his advocacy of this project was in keeping with the words that he was reported to have used the other day in Winnipeg on the occasion of an interview with the press, excepting that there were no words that required deletion and the description was "blank, blank".
I do not use language of that kind.

That is what I say with respect to that alleged interview. I, at least, have never known the minister to use language that had to be abbreviated in order to make it parliamentary. But his language was always most definite. The dam, the construction, and the irrigation were in immediate prospect, and generally the project was just around the corner.
In the by-election at Rosthern in 1948, on October 18, the minister is reported as having said that the issue of the campaign, the main task would be to push the building of the dam as soon as possible. On that occasion the Minister of Agriculture drew a picture of the development of irrigation and power on the Saskatchewan river that would result in industrial and agricultural development similar to that which I have already referred to in the Essen area of Germany.
On October 20, 1948, Mr. Tucker, speaking in the same by-election said that support had already been received from two federal cabinet ministers both of whom had expressed their favourable attitude towards the project; and he referred to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and to another minister.
On October 23,	1948, the Minister of
Agriculture said:
If this part of the country could be turned into an industrial as well as an agricultural area, it would be possible for it to support twice the population that it does now. Cheap power is the "open sesame" to industrial growth. With a dam at its


back door almost assured, and with the resultant cheap water power available in the not too distant future, Saskatoon stands at the gateway to new and unprecedented development.
And so on and so on through the years. The dam was the issue in that by-election when my hon. friend from Rosthern (Mr. Boucher) was elected. He was elected, but we did not get the dam. In 1949 it was again an issue.
There were various discussions during the years. The P.F.R.A. people went ahead with an investigation; and there are men in the P.F.R.A. who, with long training, ability and experience, know the needs of Saskatchewan. They know the needs of irrigation and they have periodically made reports to the effect that the building of this dam was not only feasible but was necessary. Moneys have been expended month by month during the last few years to determine whether or not this project should be proceeded with; and the reports by the P.F.R.A. were as clear as they were definite that this project was a proper and a feasible one. The reports so given raised the hopes of people within the province.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, January 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Knowles for the second reading of Bill No. 2. to amend the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act (voluntary revocable check-off).

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF CHAPTER 54, STATUTES OF 1947-48-VOLUNTARY REVOCABLE CHECK-OFF OF UNION DUES
speechtext:
In rising to speak to this bill, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that his introduction of it has served a very useful purpose because it has evoked an interesting debate. I should like to thank all those who took such an active part in that debate.
My hon. friend's outline of the parliamentary history of this legislative proposal since 1948 was a very fair one. I was glad that, although he thought it necessary to state that the language which forms the main part of the bill was drafted by officers of the Department of Labour, he did not try to read any unfounded significance into that fact. As a matter of fact, they did the same thing in polishing up the wording of the bill in its original form.

The hon. member spoke about Liberals standing for union security. He again made much of that fact, and it is a fact. I am one of those about whom he spoke, and I do believe in union security. I see nothing wrong in union security measures, even though I much prefer those that are freely agreed upon by labour and management. I am very pleased indeed when I learn that new collective agreements have been signed providing for union security for the first time, or extending for the second and third time the scope of previous provisions. I am pleased when these agreements have been reached freely by the two parties. My reasons for feeling that way are, first, that I am in favour of collective bargaining; second, I believe in the value of having strong and stable labour unions in Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are a good many members in this house who sincerely do not want to see employers compelled by legislation to initiate a check-off in their plants, any more than they want to see a prohibition against the union security measures in our legislation here. The question has been asked as to whether it is necessary or desirable that a responsible union should derive its stability from government imposed conditions rather than freely negotiated agreements. That, I think, is the question to which we need to give a great deal of thought and study.
In closing his speech on the motion for second reading of the bill, my hon. friend said he was encouraged by the fact that this principle has now been accepted by the railway companies and by the union representatives of many of their employees. I would say to him that the only principle the railways or the employees accepted was the principle of a negotiated check-off, freely agreed upon in the process of collective bargaining. The principle contained in the provisions of Bill No. 2 is the principle of a legislated check-off, with the word ''voluntary" applying only to the individual employee and having no reciprocal connotation for the employer.
Before I leave the subject of the settlement between the railways and their nonoperating employees, I wish to express a word of commendation to Mr. Justice Kellock and the other members of the conciliation board, to the officials representing management for the railways, and to the trade union leaders who represented the employees. Those non-operating railway labour organizations sought the adoption of the union shop, but reached agreement with management jpon the check-off of union dues.
Industrial Relations
My information is that the railways have agreed to the compulsory check-off of union dues for all members of the bargaining units for which the non-operating unions hold collective agreements, regardless of whether or not the individuals affected are members of the unions. This formula goes considerably beyond the provisions of Bill No. 2, but the important thing to remember is that it was freely negotiated.
It should not be forgotten that our law dealing with industrial relations already makes pretty secure the position of unions which by their own effectiveness and merit are able to enlist the loyalty of a majority of the workers in any given bargaining unit. The right of employees to joint unions and to carry on their lawful activities is protected, and interference and coercion on the part of employers through unfair labour practices are prohibited under penalty.
Earlier in this debate my parliamentary assistant (Mr. Cote) and also the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Macdonald) made some pertinent references to the Maintenance of Railway Operation Act which terminated the railway strike of 1950. There was universal agreement that all the elements of compulsion in that bill should disappear, and should constitute no precedent.
I am glad to say that the compulsory features of that statute have long since passed into limbo, and the parties are to be commended for having reverted to orderly collective bargaining, with enough good will on both sides to work out a settlement without disturbing industrial peace.
By any fair standard I think it will be agreed that our labour relations act is working out well. From here on I do not think any of us want parliament to impose statutory obligations upon employers and trade unions which might throw out of balance the factors of compromise and cooperation which are essential in collective bargaining. In order that collective agreements may be freely negotiated it is necessary to have a climate of good will, free from any excessive compulsion. It is that climate of good will, of mutual confidence, of willingness to conduct sincere negotiations, that the Department of Labour is ever seeking to encourage.
There are two schools of thought reflecting divergent philosophies on this matter. The views of one group are that the matter of check-off of dues is one which, in common with other conditions of employment, should be dealt with by the processes of free collective bargaining, and that legislative interference with those processes will not operate in the long run to the best interests

Industrial Relations
of the trade unions and their members. The other school of thought, as expressed in th-bill, is that the matter of the check-off of union dues is one which should be remove: from the collective bargaining field and disposed of by legislative enactment.
My parliamentary assistant, speaking of this bill on January 23 in this house, gave, in my opinion, a very clear analysis of the arguments related to this legislative proposal. For some time now the parliamentary assistant has been taking an active part, with my deputy minister and senior departmental officials, in studying the results of experience so far gained under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act.
The results of those studies may well lead in the future to proposals for amendments to the act. I do think, however, that any amendments made to this act ought to be most carefully considered and should be brought forward from time to time in groups rather than one by one in a haphazard fashion. It may be that at some future time, when a group of such amendments are brought forward, something along the lines of this bill may find its place amongst them. But we can afford, I think, to go slowly in the knowledge that the degree of industrial accord within our country is not necessarily measured by the number of laws we make on labour relations, but rather is it measured by the good will and determination of the parties concerned to find a fair solution based upon mutual confidence.
In view of the interest in this matter and having regard to the diverging views expressed, I believe that before this house is asked to vote on the principle of Bill No. 2 the bill should receive further and careful study by the competent committee of this house. I would therefore move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier):
That Bill No. 2 be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on industrial relations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to discuss this from the point of view of the proposal that is now made to refer the matter before the house to a committee. In explaining why he was introducing the amendment which he moved, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) pointed out that he did so with the idea that this would give an opportunity to consider the matter at the appropriate time. I understood him to say that this might then be dealt with at the time; that a group of amendments could be brought forward on some other occasion. If that is the situation, Mr. Speaker, the acceptance of the amendment as it now stands simply means that this proposal is shelved and that no positive steps are to be taken to have a review of the act, which is long overdue.
It will be recalled that on other occasions we have proposed that there should be a general review of this act. One of the questions that arise in regard to any single amendment of this kind is that the most desirable practice is to have a general examination of the whole act, because patching up

Industrial Relations
the act in one spot or another may not produce the desired results. In the end, as has happened on a number of other occasions, an unwieldy and sometimes incoherent act may result, and clauses introduced into the act by way of amendment from time to time may easily conflict with each other when they subsequently are interpreted by the courts or elsewhere, and they may in fact defeat the very spirit of the act itself. Often a few words introduced without regard to the whole act and the intention of the act have had the effect of defeating the very purpose for which the amendment was introduced.
If the recommendation which the minister now makes is as I understood it from his words, then the proposal before the house is simply to be put in cold storage and at some unannounced date when a general consideration of this act is to take place it might then receive consideration or might not. If there is to be a reference of any kind to a committee to deal with the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, then I suggest that this is the appropriate time to ask once again that there be a general review of the whole act. I think the time is more than ripe for such a general review.
With what the minister has said in regard to labour relations generally I think there will not be general disagreement. What has been said in response to his proposal I think will also meet with general agreement. The time is long past when there is any doubt in anybody's mind that legislation must assure the right of employees in any occupation to associate themselves together in the union of their choice, and that they must have the right to bargain collectively under clearly defined provisions when that association has been established and recognized under the terms of recognition that are placed in statutory form.
I doubt whether there is anyone today who would challenge the basic right of the employees in our different industrial and other activities of this country. One of the things which should constantly be engaging our attention is the improvement of the methods of dealing with those disputes which may arise between employees and employers, facilitating the negotiation of agreements and generally assuring that with the increased understanding of the problems of employees and employers an increasing measure of harmony may constantly be found throughout the whole of the social structure of this country.
All too often the fact that a strike may be causing some inconvenience, or that a threatened strike may actually cause great concern, obscures the extremely important

fact that in the overwhelming majority of cases the discussions between employees and employers lead to satisfactory and harmonious agreements without attracting any public attention at all. Certainly the objective of all legislation of this kind should be to increase that ever-widening area within which agreement is being so generally found.
We have advanced a long way. This is something about which there need be no partisan differences of opinion. It should be recognized that those of different political persuasions in parliament and in the other legislative bodies of Canada have year by year advanced with the wider and better understanding of employee and employer relations which has come generally to all *our people.
Most Canadians recognize today that an essential feature of the development of our social structure is the pride in work well done which finds its expression in the desire of the representatives of the employees to assure that along with every advantage they may gain from the negotiations they carry on there may also be at all times the acceptance and appreciation of the basic worth of the individual. After all I think there will be no disagreement with the statement that work well done carries with it honourable recognition on the part of every Canadian, and that in the development of this nation of ours and the improvement in the social conditions in this country there is no place where pride in a task that is undertaken can more justifiably be found than in those places where the energy, the skill and the faithful work of the individuals contribute to the general advancement of the whole country.
We are all concerned with the improvement of those conditions; we are all concerned with the general improvement of the relationship which exists. In its simplest terms, a desirable labour relations act should seek to establish, first of all, the basic right of employees to associate themselves in trade unions for the purpose of bargaining with employers and obtaining for themselves adequate wages, fair working conditions and an assurance of advancement in return for work well done. The act should also make it possible for those who represent the worker to carry out their duties on behalf of the employees in an orderly, lawful and constructive manner so that the purpose of that association of employees may be fully recognized.
A good labour relations act should be based on the thought of the mutual respect which can be established between employees and employers whenever occasion comes to carry out collective bargaining. The whole act

should follow a constructive and integrated pattern which will from time to time bring into legislative form the advances which have taken place in the relations between the employees and employers. Such an act should also be constantly under review so that from the experience which has been gained under the legislation in existence improvements may be made.
This is a subject which is of great concern not only to the members of this legislature, to employees and employers, but to the people of Canada generally. Their welfare, their daily lives are in substantial measure related to the success of legislation of this kind in producing harmony rather than dispute. It should be remembered also that a larger number of workers in Canada than those affected by legislation passed here are affected directly by legislation passed in the various provincial legislatures. Very often what is done here will offer suggestions to the provincial legislatures. Very often provincial legislatures will not deem it advisable to advance beyond the steps that have been taken by the parliament of Canada because they know there is a recognition that on the national level legislation adopted here is something that is recognized in every part of Canada.
Therefore in seeking improvements in this legislation we also can take it for granted that whatever is done here is likely also to find a response in the provincial legislatures, which most certainly have advanced greatly year by year in the legislation affecting employee and employer relations in the provinces.
I think it demonstrates something of the increasing understanding of this subject by hon. members of this house that the amendment put forward by the minister has been accepted on this occasion. Nevertheless, since reference is to be made under that amendment to the select standing committee on industrial relations, I submit that this is a good time to go beyond that. In presenting his amendment the minister has indicated that he has in mind deferring action on this until such time as a group of amendments might be brought forward. I think this is the time when consideration should be given to amendments generally which will bring the whole act into conformity with modern practices and advance the harmony of relations between employees and employers in every way possible. With that in mind I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough):
That the amendment be amended by adding thereto the following words:
"with instructions that they have power to consider and to recommend amendments to the Indus-

Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the amendment moved by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg). Knowing his feelings with respect to the bill, second reading of which has been moved by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), I think the amendment is a constructive proposal on the part of the minister. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has already indicated that it is acceptable to him. I am not the sponsor of the bill, but it is acceptable to me because I believe it is a constructive way to deal with a matter of this kind.
I think most hon. members are opposed to compulsion, but we are not so opposed to compulsion as not to pass laws compelling people to do things. As a matter of fact pretty nearly all our laws are laws of compulsion. I think someone told me that under the British system, of which we are a part, what the law does not forbid the law allows, or what the law does not compel the law permits.
I think there is a great demand for the inclusion of the provision contained in the bill before us in the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. That employers would oppose it is quite understandable because until very recent years employers have opposed organized labour in any shape or form. In that connection I remember the report made by the royal commission that investigated the textile industry around 1937 under the chairmanship of W. F. A. Turgeon. The report indicated that, with the exception of one, all the textile companies that were under review could see no reason whatsoever why they should deal with organized labour in their plants. I thought

Industrial Relations
I had conveniently in my file the statements made by the representatives of those companies, but I cannot put my hand on them now. However, I have another statement that is equally authoritative on this point.
In 1943 or 1944-I am not quite sure of the date-a commission was appointed to inquire into the national war labour board. The chairman of the commission was C. P. Mc-Tague, who was then a justice of the supreme court of the province of Ontario. The other two members were J. L. Cohen representing labour and the late Senator Bench representing employers. There were majority and minority reports, and I should like to read a quotation from the majority report which was signed by the chairman and the labour representative. It is as follows:
The recognition of the right-
The reference is to the right to bargain collectively.
-is far from universal. By far the majority of employers have resisted it over the period. Generally speaking, the great mass of employers, until comparatively recent years, have employed all weapons in their power to resist and discourage the trade union movement.
That was only too painfully recognized by those who were interested in these matters in the early years of the war. At that time almost all labour disputes were concerned with the recognition of the union in the particular employment. In order to overcome that, when the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act was drafted, right in the beginning compulsion was put on employers and employees to bargain collectively in good faith. If there is a general demand to go one step farther, and conditions being what they are, then in my opinion it is not something that should be turned down. However, I must say again that I agree with the attitude taken by the Minister of Labour, and I believe his proposal is a constructive way to deal with the matter.
I hope the industrial relations committee will meet this session, and that this matter can be discussed. If there is any desire to enlarge the scope of the committee I have no objection. It has not occurred to me that there is a general demand for a complete revamping or revision of the act, although there may be. I cannot say because I have not been as close to things in the past year or two as I would wish. I hope that this point at least can be discussed at this session. Then we would know whether sentiment was in favour of or against it. From my point of view the amendment of the minister is a much better solution than that the question should be put to a vote now and defeated as it has been on other occasions.

Mr. Speaker, at five

I had arrived at the point at which the prairie farm rehabilitation organization had determined that the proposition was feasible, and one that deserved consideration. Then there was no immediate action taken. The question arose as to whether or not the water could be secured, and whether Manitoba would be

South Saskatchewan River Project prepared to allow the diversion of the necessary waters that would be required in order to operate the irrigation plant.
The water board was set up, and apparently it arrived at a conclusion sufficiently favourable in any event to enable the project to be proceeded with. Following that, in 1949 a discussion took place in the house with reference to this matter. In order to indicate the united attitude of the opposition on that occasion, on March 29, 1949, I set out the view of the Progressive Conservative party regarding the project in these words, as they appear at page 2122 of Hansard:
This project-and it is admitted it will have the results that X have referred to-must not be used by any party as an instrument for political preferment. It should have the support of all parties to the end that it will be assured. It will be proceeded with immediately by the Progressive Conservative party when in power. Full consideration has been given to this matter. The leader of this party, having been apprised of the necessities incident to the situation not only in Saskatchewan but also in parts of Alberta and Manitoba, has given his undivided support to the plea that this work be proceeded with at the earliest date that engineering skill and capacity will permit. It should not be delayed four, seven, or ten years, but should be proceeded with now-* when this country is apparently entering into a cycle of possible unemployment, and when Saskatchewan is again facing the dangers inherent in drought. Only those who have lived in that province during the trying years of drought can appreciate that this is a work that, if proceeded with now, will give new hope to the people of Saskatchewan and to the people of western Canada as a whole. It will be a national work that will permit the expansion of industrial development, the extension of productivity in the areas affected, and will pay to the nation as a whole profits that can now only be dreamed of.
Then came the election campaign in 1949.
I am sure there was no one in Saskatchewan who did not believe that the work was going to be proceeded with, although the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when speaking in Saskatoon said that, while he was in favour of the dam, he viewed with some trepidation the danger of a dam such as was envisaged under the plan being washed out and Saskatoon being flooded.
Following the 1949 election the work preceded under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation ^ct, and several hundred holes were drilled vith a view to determining the proper loca-;ion for the dam. There were six hundred >r thereabouts in all, and everything seemed o be proceeding well to the end that the vork would be gone ahead with.
Then on May 31, 1951, for the first time o my knowledge, a suggestion was made by he Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) hat it would be necessary for the province if Saskatchewan to accept the responsibility

of providing irrigation facilities. Until that time I had never heard, nor am I able to find any record anywhere, that there was any responsibility to fall upon the province of Saskatchewan. However, the feasibility of the project was admitted by the minister, and in speaking in the house on May 31, 1951, as recorded at page 3601 of Hansard, he said -I am reading the pertinent words-
-under P.F.R.A., we had Professor Allan appointed again-
That refers to the fact that as early as 1918 Professor Allan had made a report.
-and then later on in 1947 we had another report on it which has been tabled in the house. Those reports are all favourable. I must say to the committee that all my reports to the government have been favourable, and they will continue to be favourable. I have reported to the government on each occasion we have obtained a report to the effect that in my opinion it would be a good thing to build this dam.
This year?

Three or four years ago-five years ago, for that matter-every time there has been a report. I think it would be a good thing to build this dam.
The government of Saskatchewan accepted the responsibility imposed upon it and agreed to discharge the financial responsibility incident to supplying the necessary irrigation.
Then a new wrinkle developed. We had had promises throughout the years. The dam was just around the corner at election time. Following that there were water boards set up, responsibility was placed upon the government of Saskatchewan and assumed, and then in the summer of 1951, for the first time, we found that a royal commission of experts was going to be set up to review the reports and decisions of the real experts, those who were members and officials of P.F.R.A.
The setting up of the royal commission was quite a surprise to the people of the province of Saskatchewan. After all, as far as the official opposition were concerned, we promised the minister that we would support him to the limit and without any exception would vote the necessary supply in order to permit the work incidental to the development and building of the dam to be proceeded with. So did the members of the C.C.F. party.
The royal commission was set up and empowered to inquire into the economic and social returns to be derived from the project and to measure them against the cost; and also, in effect, to ascertain whether there was not somewhere else the water could be used to better advantage. At least that is my conclusion as to the meaning of the commission report. Certainly there was nothing that would have indicated that a commission

would commence to sit and, even though only intermittently, continue to sit for an extremely long period of time, measured by the months before the report was brought down, in order to determine first, apparently, where the dam should be situated; to review the decision that had been made almost with finality as to the location of the dam; and then as well to determine whether or not the whole project was feasible, and finally, whether in the national interest the social benefits would be commensurate with the expenditure.
The commission finally brought in its report. Everyone knew what was in the report before it was tabled in parliament. For some reason the information became known in December. The general plan in connection with the dam and irrigation project was given in considerable detail. It was designed to provide for the irrigation of 455,000 acres of land in central Saskatchewan and also to provide secondary benefits:
(a)	a source of hydroelectric power for a province-wide transmission system;
(b)	a source of rural and urban water supply;
That was to supply water directly or indirectly to Regina and Moose Jaw.
(c)	stream and flood control; and
(d)	recreation facilities.
Throughout the years we who have lived in the province of Saskatchewan have known something of the terrible conditions that prevail in consequence of drought. We remember so well the year 1938. We remember years prior to that. My own memory goes back to the time we first went to Saskatchewan in 1903. Intermittently even in northwestern Saskatchewan there were periods of drought. But those people living in the areas adjacent to the elbow of the South Saskatchewan river experienced recurrent drought throughout the years. They looked forward with hope to something being done to assist them.
Now the report comes down. It is one of the most amazing documents I have ever seen. I presume what the minister said in Winnipeg was-and I am not being profane -that it was a silly damned report, because of the fact that there was a blank in the statement which he made. It is the most surprising piece of work that the ingenuity of man could possible produce, having regard to the evidence which was before them and which was available to them. The engineers and officials of P.F.R.A. had spent years looking into this matter. The minister had given his approval. He had given his benediction to the feasibility of the proposition. Members of the house in all parties were agreed that it was necessary and that it was feasible. However, when the report is brought down it consists of statements in part 68108-102
South Saskatcheiuan River Project commendatory and corroborative of the report of P.F.R.A. It speaks of the benefits that could be achieved and at times one almost concludes that the report is going to be favourable. Indeed there never was a report anywhere that could damn a project with fainter praise than did this one.
As one follows the report, one wonders what the decision will be. One can take excerpts from various parts of the report and build up a strong and powerful argument in favour of the proposition. Then after everything has been canvassed the decision finally is that it is not feasible because of the fact that we would not have a market for the garden produce that would have to be grown in order to make the irrigation expenditure worth while; that, in any event, the place chosen is indicated not to be the proper place; and that the social benefits are not commensurate with the expenditure.
The costs given are fabulously higher than those estimated by competent engineers and men in the public service who know conditions in Saskatchewan. As a matter of fact, I think it is to be regretted that the commission did not sit during years when drought afflicted our province. I cannot believe that the findings of this commission would have been as they are had the members of that commission had any knowledge of what the people in Saskatchewan suffered and of the terrible terrors of drought during the days of the 1930's until 1938. The highlights of the report are as follows, as summarized by the Canadian press:
The project is rejected as uneconomical under current conditions.
As far as that finding is concerned, it is based in large measure on what appears to be the choice of evidence that was unfavourable to the scheme. After all, when a royal commission is set up you expect it to hear both sides. You expect it to have an open mind. You expect it to face the problem that is before it by weighing the favourable evidence with the unfavourable, instead of weighing the evidence that was negative to the construction of this development. The next finding is this:
The situation might be reviewed when there is a big market for specialty crops, such as potatoes and sugar beets, in the area, or as a relief project in time of unemployment.
Mr. Speaker, I think the members of the commission, great and distinguished as they were, did not have-by reason of illness and other difficulties-the opportunity to weigh the measures that had to be considered in connection with this matter. They talk about irrigation for the production of garden stuff. We are not asking for irrigation of that kind. We are asking for irrigation that can be used

It would cost $250 million, likely to be shared B100 million by the Saskatchewan government and floO million by the federal government and Canadian taxpayers as a whole.
The evidence regarding costs is as prejudiced evidence as one could find anywhere. They chose one contracting firm that for some reason or another in some of its own tenders was twice or three times as high as the lowest tender, and that is decided upon as the company to determine the costs. As far as costs are concerned, the engineers in the Department of Agriculture had gone into that matter with thoroughness and completeness, and no one can convince me that their conclusions were almost 100 per cent wrong. More economic use could be made of the money through other projects.
That was not a conclusion they were asked to come to. We realize that the expenditure of money on some other projects -and I have none in mind at the moment- might ensure faster and surer immediate returns; but this proposition is one that would rehabilitate the province of Saskatchewan and give it a boost not only in agriculture but also in industry, without which Saskatchewan would find itself in an unequal position so far as other provinces are concerned.

Then they develop little plans and schemes, some not so little, schemes that the Minister of Agriculture has had under investigation or in contemplation during the years, some of which are under way. That very fact indicates that while the royal commission sat it was not devoting

South Saskatchewan River Project draughts. We know the benefits of irrigation. We know what could have been achieved and would be achieved if 450,000 or 500,000 acres could be irrigated for dry farming purposes within the province of Saskatchewan.
Fifth, when the royal commission says that we could not raise vegetables and sugar beets because there is no market available, it again denies the facts of history which show the benefits of irrigation to grain farming in various parts of the United States. I think this whole argument was anwered on August 9, 1951 at Outlook, Saskatchewan when the general manager of the southern Alberta eastern irrigation association, Carl Anderson, of Brooks, said that irrigation was needed in dry land farming areas. He stated also in effect that irrigation could be as beneficial to wheat and other grain farmers in Saskatchewan as it had been to farmers in other parts of North America. It has been indicated in recent years that everywhere in the world irrigation is expanding the opportunity for the production of food. Today Russia has an irrigation plan under way to irrigate some 20 million acres. Today the United States has 7 million acres under irrigation. We in western Canada have some 3 million acres which would be as productive as the best land there is, provided the necessary water was made available.
The other day we heard a speech by the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) which indicated the trend of recurring droughts and the need of irrigation and the like to assure the production of all those things. Apparently all that information was lost in so far as this royal commission was concerned. All of that was indeed ignored. One would almost conclude from reading the report that the commissioners had an objective, which was to arrive at point X. While throughout the report they describe the benefits of irrigation and state that sometime in the distant future something along this line might be done, they finally end up by claiming that this project which has been demanded by and promised to the Saskatchewan people for many years should not be built because of the costs.
I believe that we are going to get this project. Without exception we in the province of Saskatchewan are united on this matter. We demand it. We have had far too many excuses, a multiplicity of evasions and a succession of postponements. Today the people are asking for the carrying out of a promise made directly and by implication throughout the years. They are asking that it be not used again as a promise for the future; they are demanding that it be gotten under way now in these days when crop

conditions are exceptionally good for this area. They realize that history shows that inevitably periods of rainfall in that area are followed by almost corresponding periods of drought and arid non-production.
It is in order to place this matter before the house and in order to secure the opinion of members of the house that I have endeavoured to arrive at a method. So I could not proceed by way of a private member's motion. There used to be a day when private members' motions were just talked out, but now they are voted out by postponement and adjournment. I could not proceed in that way.
Within the rules the only time anything could be done was when a motion for supply came before the house. Then an opportunity is provided, and there is no other opportunity. If there were that is the method I would follow. An opportunity comes to move an amendment to the motion to go into supply. That amendment I intend to move in order to give parliament an opportunity to say what it thinks of this proposition, in order that through discussion Canadians as a whole will have some realization of what this means to us.
We have supported proposals in other parts of the country that have been for the benefit of Canada. Through the years we in Saskatchewan have been denied a fair and reasonable share of defence production because of the fact that we have not power available. Our industrial development might not be as great as that of other provinces, but with power available it would be immeasurably greater than it is. Agriculture itself with assistance would be productive in a large area.
I do not believe that the state should undertake expenditures to go into competition with private enterprise, but I do believe that the state has the responsibility of providing an equal opportunity for Canadians everywhere, and that is all we are asking in the province of Saskatchewan. So far as the report is concerned, a meticulously careful reading of it indicates that it is biased and prejudiced, unjust to our legitimate claims in that province and founded-
Time.

I was concluding, Mr. Speaker, because I want to hear the answer of the government. The newspapers say that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will speak out here in favour of this project. We want to hear why this project, justified by experience, reinforced by the evidence of the trained engineers and officials of P.F.R.A., should longer be denied to us. Without exception people in my province are asking parliament to act, not to provide alternative plans, not to start this project or that project, not to picture a vast scheme that is going to cover all Canada. They are demanding that their members from that province present their demands before parliament, demands that are legitimate, fair, reasonable and proper, and which involve in effect the implementation of promises long made and as long unkept. I therefore move, seconded by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"this house regrets that in the estimates presented to this house no provision has been made for immediately proceeding with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam."

No one questions the ability or integrity of the members of the royal commission on the South Saskatchewan river project, nor do we hold their motives in question, but I think as a member of parliament I have a duty to study the report and the soundness of its conclusions.
It seems strange to me that the commission failed to understand and appraise the agricultural, social and economic aspects of the project. The commission failed to take advantage of the wealth of factual information available in the Regina office of the P.F.R.A., information amassed by experts over a period of sixteen years, information concerning low rainfall, soil suitability, temperatures, and effects of irrigation on surrounding communities. It failed to take advantage of the advice and experience, available to it, of the officers of the P.F.R.A., their engineers and consultants, experience gained by the construction and operation of similar projects over a period of years, information on water flow, on foundation conditions, on construction of dams and irrigation canals, information and experience backed by the opinion of the most prominent engineers from the United States.
I refer here to Major General Ferguson, consultant to the United States corps of engineers on water conservation and reclamation; to Professor Casagrande of Harvard, soil expert; and to Mr. Harza of Chicago, construction engineer, who have had wide experience in the construction of such projects. The commission failed to appreciate that this is part of a plan to rehabilitate and settle that dry area of Saskatchewan and Alberta, which is the responsibility of the federal government and which responsibility will not be discharged until this project has been completed. Let me refer to some of the statements and conclusions of these men, and offer criticisms. My hon. friend who has just preceded me has gone over this in a general way, and I intend to take some of their conclusions and deal with them in detail. What a ridiculous statement!
The creation of such a tremendous reservoir by a dam will make possible an equal flow of water throughout the winter. I maintain that a reduction of power might take place on the lower Saskatchewan if the dam were not there, but on the lower Saskatchewan a dam and big reservoir of water which I mentioned before would do nothing but improve power conditions.

I wonder whether we are not to have any development of our natural resources in this country until we go back in a depression again. That would be the impression one would get from reading Mr. Richardson's summary of the findings of this commission. If that is so, this dam should have been built back in the 1930's. We had unlimited amounts of cement in Canada at that time; we had unlimited amounts of labour in Canada at that time. We were giving men ten cents a day to kill time, to carry a piece of stone from one side of the road to the other, when they could have been used in more constructive work such as this South Saskatchewan river dam; and there was certainly need for it at that time.
The need for the construction of this dam becomes more evident as you read the history of agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan over the years. In their presentation to the commission the Saskatchewan government indicated the tremendous fluctuations in agricultural income in that province over the years. In 1937, one of the worst drought years they had in that province, the total sale of farm products in Saskatchewan amounted to some $36 million. That was the cash return to the farmers of Saskatchewan in that year. Last year the return to the farmers of that province was well over $400 million, with approximately the same acreage under cultivation, which goes to show the tremendous fluctuations in production that we have in our province because of atmospheric conditions, weather conditions, over which we have no control. The building of a project such as this in the central part of the drought area in Saskatchewan, which would irrigate some 425,000 to 450,000 acres of land, would provide in the centre of the province where it is needed the fodder which would enable the province to have a more diversified agriculture. I think that is one of the strongest arguments for the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam.
The Minister of Agriculture over the years, both when he was in the province of Saskatchewan and since coming to Ottawa, has urged that in western Canada, if we are to overcome some of the difficulties with which agriculture is faced there, one of the things we must have is a greater diversification of our agricultural production. I do not agree with some of the methods which the Minister of Agriculture has been endeavouring to use over the last few years to secure that result. As a matter of fact, I think some of the methods that have been adopted have had

just the reverse effect, and that is quite evident from the decrease in production of certain of our agricultural products in western Canada. But this project would give stability to our agricultural production.
It was never suggested that this scheme, when it was first put into operation, would pay direct dividends. Practically no irrigation scheme that has ever been built has paid even the interest on the investment necessary to inaugurate the scheme during the first ten or fifteen years, yet very few of these irrigation schemes have not paid dividends in the course of twenty-five or fifty years. They have not only paid dividends in better living conditions for the people who live there, but in actual dollars and cents to the economy of the country that had the foresight, the initiative and the resources to go ahead and develop the irrigation projects and carry them to a successful conclusion.
Almost invariably the irrigation projects that have failed have been those in which the project was undercapitalized, where too great a share of the original cost was passed on immediately to the farmer who was trying to operate a unit in that irrigation district. In every case where that was done, where too large a share of the cost was passed on immediately to the operator of the farm, that scheme failed because the farmer, unable to bear that cost, became discouraged, was unable to get the necessary seed, the necessary equipment and the necessary capital to develop his individual farm and to make a financial success of it.
Where governments have had the foresight to absorb, as the central authority, the major portion of the cost of these developments, then invariably the economy as a whole has been well paid over the years through the better production and the greater consumption in that area of goods and services provided by other parts of the country. That is what would happen in the South Saskatchewan river development. It would be not only a benefit to the immediate area concerned, but to all of Canada. It would be a benefit to eastern Canada through the creation of a market for a greater share of the products of the east, the products of the factories and of the various firms which produce the agricultural implements and the services which would be required in that area. The greater production in that area would be reflected in greater freight shipments to other parts of Canada. It would be reflected in the annual statements of the railroads, of the banks, and of the other organizations which go to make up this country whose head offices are in eastern Canada but who are supplying services to western Canada. This project is
South Saskatchewan River Project not a Saskatchewan project, it is not just a western project, it is a project for Canada as a whole as well as for the people who may be situated in that particular area.
The Saskatchewan government from the beginning have been prepared to assume their fair share of the cost of this project, and that is evident from the report itself. There was a report in the press by some correspondents that would leave some doubt as to whether the Saskatchewan government, in view of the larger costs indicated in the report of the commission, would be prepared to go ahead and assume their share of those costs. I do not know how anyone could have got that impression; certainly they could not have got it if they had read the general submission by the government. Here is what the Saskatchewan government said in their submission to the commission, as appears on page 360 of the report:
I have attempted to touch on two of the major needs of agriculture in Saskatchewan (apart from market and price considerations). There is great need firstly for assured feed supplies to permit increased diversification of the economy through livestock production and. secondly, for new land on which to resettle insecure farmers.
I shall deal with that later, and I shall also deal at somewhat greater length with the question of cost.
Neither of these needs can be adequately filled without the central Saskatchewan development. Construction of this project will be a great step forward towards meeting the need for a mature and stable agricultural economy in Saskatchewan. How can we merely calculate in terms of dollars and cents what it might be worth to us. Is it any wonder that the government of this province is anxious and ready to make its investment in the project-that we are so eager to see it started.
When this press report appeared the premier of Saskatchewan wrote a letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) in which he stated quite definitely the position of the Saskatchewan government with regard to this project. He said:
In order that there may be no misunderstanding on anyone's part, may I refer you to my letter to the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner of February 10, 1951, copy of which I am enclosing. At that time the Saskatchewan government expressed its faith in the soundness of the South Saskatchewan river project and declared its willingness to meet its share of the cost. Nothing in the findings of the royal commission has altered our opinion in this regard. When the federal government is prepared to proceed with the South Saskatchewan river project, the Saskatchewan government stands ready to enter into an agreement committing itself to pay its share of the cost.
There can be no doubt that as far as the government of Saskatchewan are concerned they are prepared to go ahead with their share of this project whenever the federal government are prepared to build the dam.
