He stated that this would tend to place a great burden upon the land or upon the farmers. He goes on to indicate the various ways in which this might be divided, but he ends up by suggesting that each farm unit, which would be approximately 160 acres, would be saddled with a cost of some $70,000 for the construction of this dam and the delivery of water to the unit.
Of course that is a ridiculous cost as far as a single unit is concerned. I think it is also a ridiculous cost as far as the total project is concerned. The estimate of the engineers of the P.F.R.A. was something over $80 million for the construction of the dam, allowing for the increase in costs since the original estimate was made, and $35 million to $37 million for the cost of the water distribution system.
It is interesting to note that while the commission secured the services of the Mannix company of Edmonton to give them an estimate of the cost and the engineers of that company appeared before the commission, P.F.R.A. officials were not given an opportunity to question those costs. I think it would have been only fair for the commission to call the officials who had made the original estimate. Not only did the commission not call those engineers, apparently the government in Ottawa agreed that those officials should not be called.
On January 28 the Prime Minister answered a question which had been asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) which appears on page 1399 of Hansard and is as follows:
This commission was established to get information which the government did not already have and to make recommendations to it. As the commissioners had access to all the records and technical advice of the P.F.R.A., it was not necessary for them to have formal appearances by federal officials at public hearings. The government shared this view and gave this opinion to the officials of the P.F.R.A.
In reaching that conclusion, the government had in mind the fact that it would not be fair to place civil servants in a false position by requiring them to appear publicly and express opinions on matters on which the Minister of Agriculture and the government as a whole had subsequently to reach decisions.
It was not necessary to place the P.F.R.A. officials in that invidious position by calling them before the commission. The engineers might have been called to check the costs submitted by the Mannix company. They


had years of experience in the construction of dams-perhaps not of the size of this project-in Alberta and they had figures with regard to the costs of construction which had been obtained from other sources. They knew the cost of moving dirt in the area in which this dam was to be built. They had firsthand knowledge as to what costs in this particular area were likely to be. Surely they should have been called by the commission and allowed to check the figures given by this firm from outside the province of Saskatchewan. I am not saying that firm was not reliable, but I do think that the P.F.R.A. officials who had the knowledge of this subject and who had made previous estimates should have been called and allowed to give their evidence.
There is a reference in the report to the press by Mr. Richardson to the development of an area in the Carrot river valley triangle close to The Pas in Manitoba. He states that there are 100,000 acres there which might be developed. Not only is that project under consideration; work is actually being done there.
Neither Mr. Richardson nor the commissioners make a full recommendation as to the possibilities in that northeasterly part of Saskatchewan. As a matter of fact there are not only 100,000 acres there that can be developed. Reliable estimates have been made of that area, and it is stated that there are between 2 [DOT] 5 and 3 million acres of land there that can be developed by certain diking and drainage projects; not 100,000 acres but 3 million acres. That development is in part at least dependent on the construction of flood controls on other parts of the Saskatchewan river, and the South Saskatchewan river dam would be one of those flood control projects. This area in the northeastern part of the province of Saskatchewan and in the northwestern part of the province of Manitoba and the estuary of the Carrot and Saskatchewan rivers is flooded periodically through overflow from the Saskatchewan river in the peak of the flood of that river which usually occurs late in June when the snows are melting in the mountains.
As a result that area cannot be developed until certain flood controls are placed in the Saskatchewan river either at its headwaters or on the river at Elbow where it is proposed that this dam will be constructed. When that flood control is placed there, then it will make more easily available this 2-5 to 3 million acres of land in the northeastern part of Saskatchewan and in Manitoba. That is some of the most valuable land in the Dominion of Canada. It is the type of land that you see in the Red river valley around

the Portage plains, that you see in the Regina plains or in the Red river valley in North Dakota. It is silt land that has accumulated there over thousands of years. It is deep and productive. All that is needed is drainage and the necessary flood control measures in order to bring that land under production.
When this South Saskatchewan river dam is constructed it will make it that much easier to provide the necessary controls and to bring this huge area in the northeastern part of the province under cultivation and production. The area that it is proposed to irrigate from the South Saskatchewan river dam is not in the heart of the real drought area but on the edge of it. That is one of the reasons given by the commissioners and by Mr. Richardson in his unofficial news summary as to why the project should not be proceeded with. Nevertheless this area is so placed that it is adjacent to much of the drought area, and the construction of the dam and the irrigation of the area will enable the provision of feed for stock and feed for ranchers in the drought area itself.
The necessity for these feed banks is most apparent when one goes back and reads the history of what happened in Saskatchewan during the former drought period. In the Saskatchewan submission they say, as found at page 358 of the report of the commission:
Farmers throughout the prairie parts of Saskatchewan know only too well what a crop failure means when livestock are kept. Our worst experience was in 1937. Between September 1, 1937 and August 31, 1938, more than 450,000 tons of fodder were shipped by governmental agencies-this even after a liquidation of 611,574 cattle for canning purposes at 1-11 cents per pound had occurred.
The entire livestock population of the huge area in the central part of Saskatchewan, the southern part of Alberta and the southwestern part of Manitoba had to be liquidated in 1937 because even with the shipping of this tremendous amount of fodder into the area there still was not enough feed. They go on to say:
In that year alone more than $3,500,000 was spent in freight moving hay, feed grain and seed. We hope that this will not happen again-
Mark this.
-but in each of the years 1945, 1947, 1948 and 1949, it was necessary to ship hay into Saskatchewan to supply areas that had suffered a failure of hay crops. During that period hay was moved from The Pas, Manitoba, to Prince Albert and Saskatoon, from Brock, Alberta to Moose Jaw and Swift Current, even from the interlake country of Manitoba as far as Saskatoon, with freight charges, as far back as 1948 running to $10 per ton.
The construction of this dam would make available right in the centre of that drought area reserves of fodder which would enable farmers there to carry on more diversified
South Saskatchewan River Project agriculture, to keep livestock and to keep them with the knowledge that they were not going to have to sacrifice them for 1J cents a pound as they did in 1937 and 1938. Until we have some security in the form of additional fodder in the province of Saskatchewan, we can never have the diversified agriculture in that province that I am sure every member of parliament and every business organization in that province would like to see there.
The Saskatchewan government has itself been trying to meet some of the needs for irrigation and some of the needs for the development of better feed reserves in that province. I should like hon. members to note that in 1945-46 the department of agriculture of the province of Saskatchewan had a budget of $826,000, while in 1952-53 their budget was $3,666,000. Much of that money is being spent in the development of feed reserves for livestock in the province. The department of agriculture of Saskatchewan has set up a new conservation and development branch charged with the responsibility of undertaking the physical development of irrigation, drainage and dry land projects. This branch has an appropriation of nearly $1,350,000 for the year 1952-53.
It is well to mention that previous to the inauguration of this branch there were no engineering specialists and no equipment in the department to implement this program. Since the development of this branch engineers have been hired and the scope of the activities of the branch can be gauged by the fact that 45 water users' associations are now organized. Water has been brought to 50,000 acres of land by the province of Saskatchewan over and above the good work done by the P.F.R.A. in this regard in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. There have been 145 miles of ditch constructed,
475,000	acres of dry land projects developed, and a million acres of land affected by drainage improvements.
I could go on and give a further review of the efforts that are being made by the province of Saskatchewan to solve some of their own problems with respect to this matter but there is a limit to the resources of a province, and I believe that limit has been reached by the province in the development of the projects under their control. I am not saying they are not going to continue to spend money. They are going to continue to spend it in increasing amounts on these developments.
Their financial resources are not such that they can enter into a project of the size of the South Saskatchewan river dam and ever hope to carry the load of financing.

South Saskatchewan River Project
That is the reason we in the province of Saskatchewan are so anxious that the dominion government go ahead with this project now. We feel that it is essential as far as Saskatchewan is concerned, and that is why I think you will find at least every member from Saskatchewan on his feet expressing his views on this project, urging the federal government not to shelve the thing, not to come in with some half-hearted promise that they are going to set aside a little money to make a further survey or to make a small development with the hope that in the future -twenty years from now-this may be completed.
I hope the government will come through with something that is worth while; and that in spite of some of the unfavourable aspects of this report, the government will recognize its responsibilities. I say "its responsibilities" because it was the federal government of Canada which opened for settlement much of the drought area in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. It was while those lands were under their control that they were homesteaded and put to a use which was not a proper long-term use for those lands.
I hope the government at this session will come down with something definite; that they are accepting their responsibility and that they are going to go ahead with that development. I wish to move an amendment to the amendment moved by the hon. member
for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). His amendment read:
This house regrets that in the estimates presented to this house no provision has been made for immediately proceeding with the construction of the South Saskatchewan river dam.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue), that the amendment be amended by adding at the end thereof the following words:
as recommended by the federal government's P.F.R.A. engineers.
